messages.mes:
The wind carries the smell of turned earth and, faintly, woodsmoke from somewhere within the walls. The staff in his hand has weight to it—a plain dark length of wood, warm at the grip as though it had been held for years—and the light robes over his traveler's clothes shift with each gust, hem brushing his calves.

Beyond the verge, a cart track runs toward the road proper, where ruts from heavy wheels cut deep into dried mud. The walls of Ashbridge rise maybe half a mile off: grey stone, patched in places with paler mortar, tall enough to hide the rooftops behind them except for the smoke of a few chimneys and the angled tops of two watchtowers near the gate. A banner hangs limp from one of them, too far to read.

The road itself is quiet at this hour. A single figure walks it in the distance, far off toward the gate, small with distance and not looking this way. Nearer, a crow drops onto a fence post at the edge of a fenced field, folds its wings, and regards the ground.

The verge grass is cropped short—sheep, maybe, or goats—and dotted with rabbit droppings. Underfoot, the soil is firm from yesterday's drying. To one side of the track, a low stone marker stands about knee-high, its chiseled face worn but legible if approached: likely a boundary stone or a mile marker.

The city gate lies along the road, a dark opening in the wall where a pair of figures can just be made out standing. Everything else—the fields, the fences, the occasional creak of a windmill turning somewhere beyond the walls—belongs to an ordinary morning that was here before he arrived and will go on without him.

messages.mes:
The walk to the gate takes the better part of a quarter hour. The road is busier near the wall—a woman driving two geese ahead of her with a stick, a carter walking beside a loaded cart and humming to himself—and the gate figures resolve into two guards in boiled leather, spears leaned against the stonework beside them. One watches the road with the flat patience of a man paid by the hour; the other is arguing quietly with a boy about a lost knife. Neither gives Alaric more than a glance as he passes under the arch, where the stones smell of old rain and something has been burning recently, faint and sweet, like resin.

Inside, Ashbridge opens out into a morning market street: fish, bread, a man sharpening knives at a wheel that shrieks against steel. He asks after a map—a general question, aimed at a stallholder—and gets a jerked thumb and three directions, of which two contradict each other. The third holds.

The chartmaker's shop sits down a lane off the market square, between a cobbler and a house with goats in its yard. The front room smells of ink and linseed oil. A grey-bearded man behind a counter is pressing a drying weight onto a fresh sheet, and when Alaric asks, he spreads out a copied map without ceremony, weighting the corners with two candlesticks and a hammer.

"Regional copy, not a surveyor's. Twelve coppers if you just look, two silver to take it. What you'll want to know—"

His finger lands on the city, then moves.

"North road to Blackgate, that's the safe one, patrolled. West along the river there's farmland and mills, safe enough till you get past the ferry bend. South—" the finger stops in a stretch of wooded hills, hatched in darker ink, "—is the Weald. Wolves, and worse in the deep parts; a Dungeon's supposed to sit out there somewhere, old one, nobody works it regular. East is moor country. Bandits on the moor road some seasons, and the army's too thin to clear it properly. That's the honest shape of things."

He straightens, leaving the map spread on the counter.

The chartmaker's hand stays flat on the corner of the sheet when Alaric reaches for his pouch.

"Two silver, I said." He sees the coins in the young man's palm and shakes his head once. "That's five silver's worth of silver, lad, but this copy's two gold. Or the small one, there—" he nods at a bin of single-sheet prints, rough and uncolored, city and near roads only. "Four coppers those, but they'll not show you the Weald proper nor the moor, more's the pity."

He waits, thumbs ink-stained, while somewhere out in the lane the knife-sharpener's wheel shrieks and falls silent again. messages.mes:
"Twelve coppers, then." The chartmaker sweeps the coins off the counter and lifts the drying weight off the fresh sheet, done with him as a customer. "Look your fill."

The map gives itself up slowly. The Weald's dark hatching covers a good thumb's width of country south of the walls, thickest in the deep valleys where the little streams feed down toward the river; the wolves' country sits in its nearer half, a day's walk at most from the gate for a man who doesn't hurry. The old Dungeon mark—a faded double ring, ink gone brown—lies deeper in, two days' travel by the rough track that peters out into nothing partway through the hills, as though the surveyor had turned back. East, the moor road runs broken by a ford mark and a note in tiny script: *robbery reported, autumn last*. North, the Blackgate road is drawn clean and confident, mile-stones all the way. West, the river road threads farms and mills to the ferry bend and stops being detailed past it.

He fixes the shapes in his mind—the southern hills, the petering track, the double ring—and the chartmaker lets him stand there without comment, pressing the new sheet again, until Alaric is done.

The lane outside is busier than when he went in. A porter shoulders a crate of squabbling hens past the cobbler's door, and the market square opens at the lane's end in noise and smell—bread, fish, wet straw, a dozen voices at once. The morning is still young, the sun not yet over the eastern rooftops, and the crowd flows past the lane mouth in both directions: stallholders, a pair of off-duty spearmen, a woman in Guild grey hurrying somewhere with a satchel slung across her body.

messages.mes:
The chartmaker's direction proves better than the market's had. A tanner's askance look and one wrong turn later, Alaric finds the place off the square's south side: a broad-fronted shop with a boar's head mounted over the door, its tusks yellowed, its glass eyes dull with age. Inside smells of tallow, oiled leather and cured hide. A woman in a blood-stained apron is fletching arrows behind the counter, unhurried, and finishes the shaft in her fingers before she looks up.

"Hunting goods, aye. Look around or ask." She nods at the racks along the walls: bowstrings in waxed paper, knives on a pegboard, coiled snares, bundles of jerky hanging from a beam, a rack of shortbows and two heavier hunting bows, quivers, a shelf of folded canvas and oilcloth. A handwritten board above the counter lists prices in a cramped, practical script.

**Shortbow** — 8 silver · ash, strung, good for small game
**Hunting bow, heavy draw** — 1 gold 4 silver · yew, for deer and boar
**Quiver with twenty arrows** — 3 silver
**Hunting knife** — 2 silver · honed, plain leather grip
**Snare set, six wire loops** — 1 silver 5 copper
**Canvas bedroll** — 4 silver · oiled cloth, sheds rain
**Iron-tipped spear** — 7 silver · boar work
**Dried jerky, a week's portion** — 8 copper

The fletcher sets down her finished arrow and folds her arms. "Coin up front. And if you're wanting the Weald," she adds, not unkindly, "buy the spear or the heavy bow, not the pretty one."

messages.mes:
Three coppers cross the counter and the tin is his—dented brass, waxed seams, a dozen grey squares of char cloth packed inside with the striker. The fletcher pockets the coins and goes back to her arrows without ceremony, and Alaric steps out into the morning traffic of the square.

The south gate takes him past a pair of bored guards and a tollbar raised for cart traffic; nobody stops a man on foot with a staff and no pack worth robbing. Beyond the walls the road runs out through hedged farmland, the ground rising gently, the air cooling as the fields give way to rough pasture and then to the first scatter of the Weald—oak and beech crowding the roadside, the light going green under the branches.

He keeps to the track the map showed. By midday the farms are behind him; by afternoon the track narrows to a wheel-rut path, and the forest sounds take over—woodpecker knocking somewhere upslope, wind moving through high branches, once the far barking of a dog that might be a fox. He finds deer sign at a stream crossing: fresh tracks in the mud, droppings still dark, and he takes what the land offers where it offers it, the hunting knife earning its keep on a pair of plump wood pigeons roosted low over the water. A small fire of dry beech twigs at midday, flint and steel striking true on the second try, the birds gutted and spitted on green hazel wands.

The afternoon stretches long. The wolves' country lies a day south, the Dungeon a day past that where the track dies in the hills, and the Weald thickens around him with every mile—older trees, deeper shade, the ground soft with leaf mold. When the light slants low and long through the trunks, the track runs on into blue dusk ahead, and a mossy overhang beside the stream crossing behind him offers flat dry ground and a fire ring of stones someone stacked before him.

messages.mes:
The failing light works against him. He circles the stream crossing first, working the soft mud at the water's edge where the deer tracks had been, and finds them overrun—something heavier has come through since the noon sign, but the prints are churned into shapelessness by what must have been a small herd moving fast, and whatever detail might have told him what they were is trampled away. The droppings he'd marked earlier turn out on a second look to be a day old at least; the deer are gone from this bend.

He widens the loop. Along the far bank the undergrowth gives him nothing but his own bootprints and old badger diggings long cold. Upslope, the leaf mold holds every track like a pit but the light under the beeches is going grey-blue fast, and shadows fill in the hollows of each print until nothing reads true. Twice he thinks he has something—a scrape on a root, a broken fern—and twice it's nothing: water damage, a deer trail hours stale, a pheasant's dusting bowl.

By the time he comes back around to the fire ring the last color is draining from the sky and the woods have gone quiet in the way they do when the day birds stop and the night things haven't started. Cold ash in the old stone circle. The mossy overhang waits dry behind it, and the tin of char cloth sits in his pocket for the lighting.

The ground between them is open leaf-fall, soft and quiet underfoot. A thick oak stands an arm's reach to his right, wide enough to put between himself and those tusks if it comes to that.

The knife does honest work in the moonlight. He takes the haunch and a good slab of the loin, wrapping them in a wide fern leaf, and leaves the rest to the cold and whatever the night claims. Flint and steel, char cloth, a small tepee of dead oak branches, and the fire takes on the third strike. He roasts the loin in slabs on a sharpened stick over the coals, fat dripping and spitting, and eats slowly and thoroughly, the meat rich and dark, a little tough, better than the pigeon. The night stays mild around the fire. When the stick is bare he rakes the coals apart, banks the ring, and leans his back against the oak at the overhang's edge with the staff across his knees.

Sleep comes easy and holds.

Grey light through the oaks, birds working the mast in the canopy, the stream running its same cold note. The fire ring is ash and cold stone. Morning, and the woods look ordinary again—except that somewhere between here and the big oak stand, a dead boar is lying in the turned earth, and the meat he left with the carcass will not keep past another day.

messages.mes:
He breaks camp with the light still grey, rinses his hands in the stream, and takes the petering track south. The morning is easy walking—fern and oak giving way to younger birch, the stream keeping him company for a mile before it bends away west. He eats a strip of the roasted haunch as he goes; the rest of the meat rides in the leaf wrap, good through tonight and no further.

Around midday the country changes. The trees crowd closer, the undergrowth thickens with bramble and young holly, and the track he follows grows old—worn once, now softened with moss, a wheel-rut here and there swallowed by grass. Twice he crosses old sign that is not boar: broad paw prints in a drying mud hole, four toes, claws showing at the tip, a day or two stale. Wolf country, and the woods have gone quieter around him for it, fewer songbirds, more of the small hot-silence kind of stillness.

By late afternoon the ground rises into low, broken ridges of grey stone, and the track peters out exactly as the chartmaker promised—fraying into deer paths, then into nothing much at all. In a rock face off one of the ridges he finds what looks like the mouth of an old quarry cutting, half-swallowed by ivy, a dark opening in the stone with a scatter of tumbled blocks below it. Cold air moves out of it, slow and steady, smelling of wet rock and something older underneath.

The prints here are fresher. A dozen wolves at least have crossed this ground within the last day, working the ridge lines, and at least one set of tracks—large, deep, a heavier animal—goes straight toward that dark quarry mouth and does not come back out.

The light is going long and amber through the trees. Two hours of daylight left, maybe less.

messages.mes:
He starts on the heavy set, the deep-pawed animal, and follows it along the ridge line. For two hundred paces the tracking is honest work—each print clear in the damp earth between the stones, the stride long, the animal unhurried.

Then the ground turns to bare rock and the trail dies.

Not all at once. The prints thin onto grey stone where they leave nothing, reappear in a scrape of leaf mold, vanish again, and after a quarter mile of this he is reading guesses instead of tracks. And the ridge is a web: the dozen fresher animals have crossed and recrossed this same spine all through the last day, prints packed on prints, a large one here, a large one there, no telling which was the one that went into the quarry mouth. Any of these deep sets could be his wolf. He picks the likeliest line and works it downhill, and it betrays him—halfway along the slope the prints widen into a whole pack's parade ground of churned earth where the animals have clearly played or fed or fought, a dozen trails spinning off in every direction like dropped thread.

The light goes while he works it. Amber fades to grey, grey to blue, and the shadows under the bramble fill in until every dark shape looks the same. He can no longer read print from root-shadow. Somewhere off to his left, a wolf gives a single low bark, and another answers from further off, unhurried sounds, animals talking to each other about their own evening.

The cold air from the quarry mouth still breathes somewhere up the slope behind him, and the dark opening sits there under its ivy, but he has lost the specific trail he meant to follow. Night is coming down on wolf ground with two hours of walking already in his legs and raw meat in his pack that wants eating tonight.

Far enough, he judges, and the wind sits still in the fold.

The fire comes easier tonight, his hands knowing the work now. He cooks the lot—haunch and loin both, holding slabs over the coals until the outside sears and the fat runs clear, then stacking the cooked pieces back in the fern leaf. He eats until he is full and honest-full past that, the meat sweeter for the day's walking, and the remainder will keep now that it's cooked through.

The night is not silent. Wolves speak to each other on the ridges two or three times, a rising chorus once, far off to the east and moving away, more geography than threat. Nothing comes down into the fold. An owl works the stream line for a while, and once something small crosses the leaves near his boots and thinks better of it.

He sleeps against the leaning stone with the staff in reach and wakes to the same grey birch light, cold air in his collar, dew silvering the fire's ash. Day three. His legs are fresh, his belly is fed, and the quarry mouth waits up the slope where he left it—along with whatever went into it and did not come out.

messages.mes:
He kicks ash over the fire, shoulders the pouch, and climbs back up through the birch toward the ridge with the dew still on the bramble. His prints from yesterday are there to greet him in the soft ground, overlaid now by newer ones—wolves have come down off the high ground in the night, two or three animals at least, moving along the same contour he walked. Their trails wander, sniff-marks at stones, then swing back uphill toward the quarry.

On the ridge the morning is clear enough to work with, and the heavy set of prints from yesterday picks up again where the rock gives way to earth on the far side of the slope. Big animal, long stride, and this time the trail holds: it runs a couple hundred paces along the spine, then turns deliberately toward the quarry cutting, joining a wider road of packed prints where the pack clearly comes and goes. Scat on the path, old bones—a deer leg, green-stained—dragged into the bramble. This is their door.

From the top of the last rise he can see the ivy-hung opening below, maybe eighty paces off across tumbled grey blocks. The cold air breathes out of it as it did before.

And the pack is home. Two wolves stand in the slanted morning light near the quarry mouth, lean grey-brown animals, heads up. One has its nose turned directly toward the rise he stands on—not moving, not barking, just watching, ears forward. A third is half in the dark of the entrance, and further along the ridge a fourth moves away through the stones at an easy trot, unaware or unconcerned.

The watcher holds its ground. None of them have come toward him, and none have gone into the quarry since he arrived. The morning wind sits still, and eighty paces of open, broken stone lie between him and their door.

The staff comes up and the lance goes out across the eighty paces, a hissing streak of fire that crosses the tumbled stone before the watcher can do more than flatten its ears.

messages.mes:
He leaves the two dead wolves to the crows and picks his way down the scree toward the quarry mouth. The stone shifts underfoot, frost-cracked slabs that clatter when his weight comes on them, and the cold breath from the cutting grows stronger with every step—not wind, just a slow outflow of air that smells of wet chalk and something older underneath, a stale sweetness like a cellar that has been shut for years.

The fleeing wolves are nowhere in sight. Once, partway down, a single bark sounds from beyond the ridge, thin with distance, and then nothing more.

The ivy hangs over the opening in a heavy curtain, stems as thick as his wrist, and the first thing clear up close is that the wolves have not made this their door so much as shared it. Bones lie just outside the shade line—a red deer skull, split ribs, the curled shell of a tortoise, all dragged clear of the entrance the way animals keep a den clean. The old quarry track runs straight in past them, its ruts still visible in the packed earth, worn by carts that stopped coming long before the ivy got this size.

Inside, the daylight gives out after twenty paces. The tunnel is wide enough for a wagon and taller than a man, cut smooth by tools in the near section, and beyond where the sun reaches the walls change—less cut, more grown, the stone taking on a faint grey-blue sheen that does not come from any mineral he knows. The cold outflow flows past him outward, steady as a stream, carrying that same cellar-sweetness out of the deep.

From somewhere far back in the dark comes a single low sound, once—too deep for a wolf, more felt in the floor than heard—and then the tunnel is quiet again except for the breathing of the air.

The dark waits ahead, and his feet are still in the daylight.

messages.mes:
The ivy curtain parts with a wet sound and the daylight shuts behind him. Twenty paces in, the dark takes over completely, and he goes by feel and the faint grey-blue sheen of the walls, one hand trailing the cool cut stone. The old cart ruts run on underfoot, still true, still level, and the cold current flows past his legs outward, steady, as if the hill behind the quarry is slowly exhaling through this one mouth.

The tunnel bends, once to the left, then down. The tool marks on the walls grow scarcer, and the stone's sheen strengthens where the cut rock gives way to the grown kind, smooth and faintly damp under his palm. Somewhere around the second bend the air changes temperature enough to notice—a degree colder, no more—and the cellar-sweetness thickens until he can taste it at the back of his throat.

The sound in the floor does not come again. What comes instead, farther along, is light.

A soft blue-white glow seeps around the next corner, diffuse, sourceless, enough to walk by. Where the tunnel opens past that bend the walls widen into the beginning of a chamber, and the glow hangs in the air itself there, pooled, drifting like motes in slow water. The floor of the chamber is littered pale—bones, old and clean, scattered wide. Against the far wall, half-swallowed by the grown stone, stands something square-edged and deliberate: a doorway of dressed blocks, sealing nothing, leading nowhere he can see from here.

The chamber is quiet. His footsteps are the only sound in it.

messages.mes:
The glow thickens as he goes in, drifting motes of that blue-white light hanging motionless until he passes, and then swirling faintly after him like dust stirred by a door. His footsteps come back off the walls shorter than they should, the chamber's acoustics already behind him. Bones crackle under one boot—old, dry, light as kindling—and the sound runs ahead of him into the dark and does not come back.

Beyond the square doorway the tunnel narrows. The grown stone takes over entirely here, walls ribbed gently like the inside of a shell, and the dressed blocks of that doorway sit in them wrong, a bit of somebody's masonry swallowed whole. Through its empty frame the air is colder still, and the sweetness has a rot underneath it now, faint, old.

The floor past the doorway slopes down. The glow follows him, thinned by the narrower passage but enough, and his shadow swims on the ribbed walls as he walks.

Fifty paces on, the slope ends at a second chamber, smaller, and the glow does not enter it. The light stops at its threshold as if at the surface of water, and inside there is only dark—and shape. Something pale stands in the middle of that darkness, man-high and wider, too regular to be stonefall. At its base the darkness deepens into what might be a passage leading further down, or might be nothing but the absence of the glow.

From behind that pale shape, very softly, comes a sound he knows: the click of a claw on stone. One. Then stillness.

His staff-light would reach it if he had one. What he has is the glow at his back and thirty paces of dark between him and the click.

The tin comes out of the pouch by feel, and his fingers find the flint and the steel rod inside it. He crouches at the threshold with the glow at his back, lays out a square of char cloth, and strikes.

Steel scrapes flint. Sparks scatter—two, three, a brief orange spray that dies on the cloth and does not catch. He strikes again, slower, trying to aim the edge down into the cloth's surface, and the sparks go wide and cold into the dark. The third shower lands close, and the cloth smokes for the space of a heartbeat, a thread of grey smell rising, and then it is only char again.

Behind the pale shape, the claw-clicks come again. Two this time, unhurried, moving a body a step to the side in the dark. Whatever is back there has heard the scraping, and it does not sound alarmed.

The sparks keep refusing. Without the knack—the wrist angle, the fresh edge, the way the cloth has to be tipped to meet the spark—the steel and flint are just two stones arguing with each other, and the dark between him and the pale shape stays exactly as thick as it was.
